Below is a complete empirical plan tailored to your setup.

1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Fuzzy regression discontinuity design (FRD) at the age-65 Medicare eligibility cutoff.
- Rationale: Age is an as-good-as-random running variable at the precise 65th-birthday cutoff. Insurance coverage jumps discontinuously at 65 (sharp first stage), while health and health-care needs evolve smoothly with age over short windows. FRD recovers the local average treatment effect (LATE) of gaining insurance on hospital admissions for compliers at the threshold. We will:
  - Estimate the reduced-form jump in hospital admission rates at age 65.
  - Estimate the first-stage jump in insurance coverage at age 65 (using NHIS).
  - Form the Wald ratio to obtain the FRD LATE of insurance coverage on hospital admissions.
- Complement: Also report the reduced-form effect of Medicare eligibility on admissions, which is policy-relevant in its own right.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable: Insurance coverage indicator (covered by any insurance; in practice, Medicare) at the individual level. For the LATE, we use coverage (from NHIS) as the endogenous treatment.
- Control group: Individuals just below age 65 (e.g., 63–64.99), who are ineligible for Medicare.
- Treated group: Individuals just at or just above age 65 (e.g., 65.00–66.99), who become eligible for Medicare and experience a discrete increase in coverage.
- Treatment timing/event: Exact 65th birthday (Medicare eligibility begins the first day of the month you turn 65; we therefore prefer monthly/quarterly age if available).
- Running variable and cutoff: Running variable x = age (in quarters or years) relative to 65; cutoff c = 0 (at age 65). If quarters are available, we use age-in-quarters for sharper RDD; otherwise age-in-years.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of Medicare, the potential hospital admission rate would evolve smoothly with age at 65. Plausible: clinical risk changes with age are gradual; no intrinsic clinical jump exactly at the birthday.
- No precise manipulation of the running variable: Individuals cannot strategically change their age relative to 65. Plausible: date of birth is fixed; age measurement in surveys/administrative data is not manipulable at fine scales. We will verify no discontinuity in the population age density at 65.
- First-stage discontinuity: Insurance coverage exhibits a large jump at 65. Plausible and documented in NHIS; we will estimate it directly (expect ~10–12 pp).
- FRD LATE conditions: Monotonicity (turning 65 weakly increases insurance for everyone—no one loses coverage because they turn 65); exclusion at the margin (crossing the cutoff affects admissions only through insurance, while other determinants vary smoothly). Plausible: The main discrete change at 65 in health-care access is Medicare coverage; retirement and health preferences evolve smoothly by age, with no mechanical birthday jump.
- Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): One person’s Medicare eligibility at 65 does not affect another’s admissions locally. Plausible in this context.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Threat 1: Confounding discontinuities at age 65 (e.g., retirement, Social Security, physician behavior). Mitigation:
  - Use a narrow bandwidth (e.g., 2–3 years or fewer; prefer quarters/months) with local linear RD and triangular kernel.
  - Show continuity at 65 for covariates from NHIS (sex, race, education, marital, region) and for “placebo outcomes” unlikely to respond to insurance (e.g., emergency trauma admissions like MVAs).
  - Placebo RD cutoffs at nearby ages (63, 64, 66, 67).
- Threat 2: Coarse running variable (age-in-years) creates measurement error around the cutoff. Mitigation:
  - Prefer age-in-quarters if available; otherwise use bias-corrected RD (Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik), try donut RD excluding those recorded exactly at age 65 in years, and show robustness to bandwidth choices.
  - Use binned RD plots with optimal bins to visualize continuity and the jump.
- Threat 3: Population composition and denominator issues when using discharge records. Mitigation:
  - Construct hospital admission rates per 1,000 population by single-year-of-age (merge with Census single-year-of-age population counts; state-specific for OSHPD).
  - Check continuity in the age distribution from Census at 65 using an RD density test (rddensity) to ensure no spurious denominator jumps.

5. R Code Outline
Notes:
- This outline uses rdrobust and rddensity. It computes (i) first-stage (NHIS), (ii) reduced-form (OSHPD California admissions per 1,000), and (iii) FRD LATE via the Wald ratio with delta-method SEs. Replace file paths/column names as needed.
- If you have age in quarters (age_qtr), set use_quarters = TRUE. Otherwise it will fall back to age in years.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(rdrobust)
library(rddensity)
library(ggplot2)

# 0. Controls
use_quarters <- FALSE  # set TRUE if age-in-quarters available in your files
min_age <- 60
max_age <- 70
cutoff <- 65

# 1) FIRST-STAGE: NHIS (insurance vs age)
# Assume NHIS.csv has: age_year (or age_qtr), insured (0/1), weight (survey weight)
nhis <- fread("NHIS.csv")

if (use_quarters && "age_qtr" %in% names(nhis)) {
  nhis[, x := age_qtr - cutoff]  # e.g., 64.75 means one quarter below 65
} else {
  nhis[, x := age_year - cutoff]
}
nhis <- nhis[x >= (min_age - cutoff) & x <= (max_age - cutoff)]

# First-stage RD (coverage jump at 65)
fs <- rdrobust(y = nhis$insured, x = nhis$x, weights = nhis$weight, kernel = "triangular")
print(fs)

# 2) OUTCOME: OSHPD (California hospital admissions per 1,000 population)
# OSHPD.csv has at least: age_year (or age_qtr), year, discharge_id; optionally emerg_flag, dx/proc, payer
# CENSUS.csv has: state, year, age_year, population
oshpd <- fread("OSHPD.csv")
census <- fread("CENSUS.csv")

# Keep California and study years
oshpd[, state := "CA"]
census <- census[state == "CA"]

if (use_quarters && "age_qtr" %in% names(oshpd)) {
  # Aggregate OSHPD discharges by age_qtr across all years (summing numerators and denominators across years)
  oshpd_age <- oshpd[, .N, by = .(age_qtr)]
  # For population denominators at quarterly age, approximate by linear interpolation from single-year ages
  # Create interpolated population by quarters
  pop_age <- census[, .(pop = sum(population)), by = .(age_year)]
  # Interpolate to quarters
  pop_age <- pop_age[order(age_year)]
  # Build a data.table of quarter grid
  age_qtr_grid <- data.table(age_qtr = sort(unique(oshpd_age$age_qtr)))
  age_qtr_grid[, age_floor := floor(age_qtr)]
  age_qtr_grid[, frac := age_qtr - age_floor]
  pop_age[, pop_lead := shift(pop, type = "lead")]
  pop_interp <- merge(age_qtr_grid, pop_age, by.x = "age_floor", by.y = "age_year", all.x = TRUE)
  pop_interp[is.na(pop_lead), pop_lead := pop]  # boundary handling
  pop_interp[, pop_qtr := (1 - frac) * pop + frac * pop_lead]
  oshpd_age <- merge(oshpd_age, pop_interp[, .(age_qtr, pop_qtr)], by = "age_qtr", all.x = TRUE)
  oshpd_age[, rate := 1000 * N / pop_qtr]
  oshpd_age[, x := age_qtr - cutoff]
  oshpd_age <- oshpd_age[x >= (min_age - cutoff) & x <= (max_age - cutoff)]
  yvec <- oshpd_age$rate; xvec <- oshpd_age$x; wvec <- oshpd_age$pop_qtr  # weight by population
} else {
  # Aggregate discharges and population by single-year-of-age across all available years
  oshpd_ageyr <- oshpd[, .N, by = .(age_year)]
  pop_ageyr <- census[, .(population = sum(population)), by = .(age_year)]
  ca_age <- merge(oshpd_ageyr, pop_ageyr, by = "age_year", all.x = TRUE)
  ca_age <- ca_age[age_year >= min_age & age_year <= max_age]
  ca_age[, rate := 1000 * N / population]
  ca_age[, x := age_year - cutoff]
  yvec <- ca_age$rate; xvec <- ca_age$x; wvec <- ca_age$population  # weight by population
}

# Reduced-form RD: jump in admissions at 65
rf <- rdrobust(y = yvec, x = xvec, weights = wvec, kernel = "triangular")
print(rf)

# 3) FRD LATE via Wald ratio (independent samples => cov ~ 0)
tauY <- rf$Estimate["tau.us"]     # point estimate of reduced-form jump
seY  <- rf$se["tau.us"]
tauD <- fs$Estimate["tau.us"]     # first-stage jump in coverage
seD  <- fs$se["tau.us"]

late <- as.numeric(tauY / tauD)
# Delta-method SE (independent samples)
se_late <- abs(late) * sqrt( (seY / tauY)^2 + (seD / tauD)^2 )
cat(sprintf("FRD LATE (effect of insurance on admissions per 1,000): %.3f (SE = %.3f)\n", late, se_late))

# 4) Diagnostics and robustness

# 4a) Density test at the cutoff (no manipulation) using Census age distribution
if (exists("ca_age")) {
  rdd <- rddensity(X = ca_age$x, w = ca_age$population)
  summary(rdd)
  # Optional plot
  # rdplotdensity(rdd, ca_age$x)
}

# 4b) Placebo cutoffs
placebo_ages <- c(63, 64, 66, 67)
for (pc in placebo_ages) {
  if (exists("ca_age")) {
    xpl <- ca_age$age_year - pc
    placebo <- rdrobust(y = ca_age$rate, x = xpl, weights = ca_age$population, kernel = "triangular")
    cat(sprintf("Placebo cutoff at %d: tau=%.3f, se=%.3f, p=%.3f\n",
                pc, placebo$Estimate["tau.us"], placebo$se["tau.us"], placebo$pv["tau.us"]))
  } else {
    xpl <- oshpd_age$age_qtr - pc
    placebo <- rdrobust(y = oshpd_age$rate, x = xpl, weights = oshpd_age$pop_qtr, kernel = "triangular")
    cat(sprintf("Placebo cutoff at %d (quarters): tau=%.3f, se=%.3f, p=%.3f\n",
                pc, placebo$Estimate["tau.us"], placebo$se["tau.us"], placebo$pv["tau.us"]))
  }
}

# 4c) Bandwidth and donut robustness
# Narrower bandwidth
rf_h2 <- rdrobust(y = yvec, x = xvec, weights = wvec, kernel = "triangular", h = 2)
print(rf_h2)
# Wider bandwidth
rf_h5 <- rdrobust(y = yvec, x = xvec, weights = wvec, kernel = "triangular", h = 5)
print(rf_h5)

# Donut RD (drop observations very near 65 if using coarsened age-in-years)
if (exists("ca_age")) {
  donut <- ca_age[age_year != 65]
  rf_donut <- rdrobust(y = donut$rate, x = donut$x, weights = donut$population, kernel = "triangular")
  print(rf_donut)
}

# 4d) Heterogeneity (optional): emergency vs non-emergency
# If emerg_flag (1=emergent) exists, recompute rates separately and rerun rdrobust for each subset.
```

6. Expected Results
- Direction: Admissions increase at age 65 due to improved coverage and lower out-of-pocket costs; increases concentrated in elective/non-emergent and procedure-oriented care.
- Magnitude (prior): Reduced-form jump in admissions per 1,000 population likely positive; a 2–6% increase in overall admissions rate is plausible locally. First stage ~10–12 pp increase in coverage implies an IV estimate (per 1 pp coverage) equal to roughly (0.2–0.6)% change in admissions, translating to a several-percent higher utilization for newly insured compliers. Expect larger effects among groups with higher pre-65 uninsurance.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
- C1: No precise manipulation of running variable at cutoff (age) — 1
- C2: Continuity of potential outcomes/covariates at cutoff (verified via covariate/placebo checks) — 1
- C3: Strong first stage (coverage jump at 65) — 1
- C4: Appropriate functional form/bandwidth with robust bias-correction and kernel weighting — 1
- C5: No other discontinuous confounders at 65 (retirement, etc., evolve smoothly; placebo cutoffs support) — 1

Notes and extensions
- Use NIS as a national complement: construct national admissions rates per age using NIS discharge weights and national Census populations; replicate the RD and compare to California results.
- If exact month-of-age is available (some states have finer age bins), prefer age-in-months/quarters to sharpen estimates and reduce attenuation from coarsening.
- Consider separate analyses by race/ethnicity, ZIP-income quartiles, and insurance type shares to illuminate mechanisms.
